title: A blessed night
hook: We sent it down on a blessed night (44:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, friends that day: the verse that says close friends turn into enemies on the last day, except the mindful. Your line was friends in goodness last. Did you get time with one of them? Day five hundred seventy-two.

Plenty of books never say when they were written. The Qur'an speaks of its own coming down more than once, and here it names not a year or a season but a night. Today we open Surah Ad-Dukhan, the Smoke, the forty-fourth surah. It begins with two Arabic letters, Ha and Mim, whose meaning, scholars say, Allah knows best, then an oath by the book itself, and then, in the third verse, a time stamp. Not a date. A quality. The night it came down was blessed.

Pickthall's translation of the opening: "Ha. Mim. By the Scripture that maketh plain. Lo! We revealed it on a blessed night." The Arabic for blessed night is laylatin mubarakah. Mubarak comes from baraka, a word you may know from a greeting card: Eid Mubarak. Baraka is blessing that stays and grows, the way a little food somehow feeds a whole table. So which night is it? Ibn Kathir and most commentators say it is the same night named in Surah Al-Qadr, the ninety-seventh surah: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, which hadith place in the last ten nights of Ramadan. Surah Al-Baqarah also says the Qur'an was revealed in the month of Ramadan, and putting those verses together, that reading became the common one. A minority of early voices connected this verse to the middle night of Sha'ban instead, and some Muslims still keep that night with prayer, but Ibn Kathir and others held to Ramadan. The verse right after says that on this night every wise matter is made distinct, and commentators read that as the affairs of the coming year being set out, part of why people spend that night in prayer. Then there's the timing itself. Why a night at all? The Qur'an keeps coming back to the dark hours: rising for prayer while others sleep, verses that speak of the night as a covering. A night is when the noise stops. The sources don't explain why this book arrived after sunset rather than at noon, and it's honest to say so. But the people who keep the Night of Power answer with their feet: they stay awake, they pray, they read, waiting for a night that is better than a thousand months.
screen: `HA. MIM. AN OATH BY THE BOOK.` · `MUBARAK: BLESSING THAT STAYS AND GROWS.` · `MOST SAY: THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `A NIGHT, WHEN THE NOISE STOPS.`

segments.voice: One minute in the night is the practice, but you may be hearing this at noon, so start with the minute you have. Sit, and let the room go quiet. Picture the last real dark you remember: a sleeping house, one lamp, nobody needing you. Breathe there. If you pray, you can choose a minute tonight, after everyone is asleep, to pray or to say alhamdulillah slowly. If you don't, set an alarm for one minute of stillness before bed. The bell holds the time.
A blessed night. Laylatin mubarakah: the night the Qur'an came down, which most commentators identify with the Night of Power in Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: a blessed night. Tonight, before you sleep, take one minute in the dark with no screen, and notice what the quiet sounds like. Day five hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims spend the odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan in extra prayer and Qur'an reading, seeking Laylat al-Qadr; some also keep the middle night of Sha'ban, and many pray a short night prayer before dawn year round.
